To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a mixed system is preferable to a PAYG system, and that the introduction of a mixed pension system, in anticipation of a negative shock is preferable to the introduction of a PAYG system after a negative shock.

a PAYG system is not the best solution for a society, even if it is introduced after a large aggregate shock, but a mixed system would be better, and that a mixed system is even better than a PAYG system if it is introduced before the shock.

(i) a fully funded system is not dynamically efficient, since it suffers from a moral-hazard problem, (ii) the introduction of a mixed pillar, in the form of a PAYG system, reduces the moral-hazard problem but is not dynamically efficient either, since the PAYG system is not Pareto efficient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of the social security system, in a dynamic stochastic economy with political constraints.
the interaction between aggregate shocks, political constraints and social security design.
the political economy of social security design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, when political constraints are present and the aggregate risk is relevant, the introduction of a mixed (fully-funded and unfunded) social security system may be preferable to a fully funded system.
a mixed system is the best option for a country with a PAYG pension system, but only if the country has already a mixed system in place.
the introduction of a mixed pension system is not a good idea, since it does not solve the moral hazard problem, but it introduces a new problem: the inefficiency of the unfunded system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the introduction of a mixed pension system would not only reduce moral hazard problems, but also reduce the size of the PAYG component.
the presence of political constraints may induce the introduction of an unfunded pillar in the system.
, when political constraints are binding, the design of a social security system must take into account the possibility of policy-makers intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the introduction of a mixed social security system is a Pareto improvement with respect to the case of no intervention, but it does not eliminate the moral hazard problem.
, when political constraints are present, the design of a mixed system is not a second best, but it is the best possible solution.
political constraints can lead to a moral hazard problem in the choice of the portfolio of a fully funded pension system.
